subject: Geography
central_question: How are India’s mineral and energy resources classified and distributed, how are they used, and why must exhaustible resources be conserved while renewable alternatives are developed?
in_scope_units: Definition, classification and characteristics of minerals
Major mineral belts and the geological pattern of mineral distribution
Ferrous minerals: iron ore and manganese
Conventional energy resources: coal, petroleum and natural gas
Nuclear energy resources and major nuclear power projects
Non-conventional energy sources: solar, wind, tidal, wave, geothermal and bio-energy
Conservation of mineral resources through recycling, substitution and reduced waste
banned_topics: Detailed manufacturing-industry location, which belongs to industrial geography
Detailed international commodity trade and ports, which belong to International Trade

known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter includes organic mineral fuels such as coal and petroleum as well as inorganic non-metallic minerals such as mica and limestone.
Ferrous minerals contain iron; non-ferrous metallic minerals do not contain iron.

known_pitfalls.claim: Minerals can be replenished quickly when demand rises.
known_pitfalls.correction: They form over long geological periods and are exhaustible, so they cannot be replenished immediately.

known_pitfalls.claim: Nuclear energy is listed with renewable non-conventional sources.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter treats nuclear minerals as conventional exhaustible energy resources, while solar, wind, hydro-geothermal and biomass are renewable alternatives.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Exercise 1(i) to locate the major oil-field state among the options.
Use NCERT Exercise 2(i) to organise the distribution of mica.
Use NCERT Exercise 2(ii) to connect nuclear minerals with major power stations.
Use NCERT Exercise 2(iv) to define non-conventional energy sources.
Use NCERT Exercise 3(i) to write a structured account of petroleum resources.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with EXERCISES 1–3: three MCQs, four short-answer questions and two long-answer questions.
